comparisons.peer_topic: Hyperscale Customer Base and Product Applications
comparisons.peer_summary: AMD's data center products, including server CPUs, GPU accelerators, and adaptive SOCs, are purchased by large public cloud providers and hyperscale private data centers. These customers incorporate the products into servers for web applications, public cloud services, and AI workloads such as generative AI models.
comparisons.comparison: Both companies describe their data center platforms as critical infrastructure for hyperscale and public cloud customers, specifically highlighting AI workloads. NVIDIA frames its Data Center platform as a comprehensive system (compute, networking, software) delivered as modules to accelerate AI and HPC, explicitly contrasting its performance and power efficiency against CPU-only approaches. AMD describes its data center products (CPUs, GPUs, accelerators) as being purchased by large public cloud providers and incorporated into servers to support these same AI workloads. While NVIDIA emphasizes the integrated nature of its accelerated computing platform versus conventional CPUs, AMD focuses on the adoption of its specific product mix (including CPUs and GPUs) by hyperscale customers for cloud and AI services.

sentences.text: The NVIDIA Data Center platform is focused on accelerating the most compute-intensive workloads, such as AI, data analytics, graphics and scientific computing, delivering significantly better performance and power efficiency relative to conventional CPU-only approaches.
It is deployed in cloud, hyperscale, on-premises and edge data centers.

Large multi-national public cloud service providers and hyperscale private data centers directly and indirectly purchase a substantial portion of our data center-focused products, including server CPUs, GPU accelerators, DPUs, FPGAs and Adaptive SOCs.

Hyperscale data centers use these products to operate web-based applications or to support public cloud computing and storage service offerings, including but not limited to AI workloads such as generative AI models.

peer_results.rationale: The provided candidates (avgo_2024_1_D025, avgo_2024_1_D023) focus on private cloud infrastructure software (VMware) and license portability, which is a software-defined networking/virtualization topic, rather than the hardware-based AI and HPC compute acceleration platform described by NVIDIA in Item 1.

The provided candidates (intc_2024_1_D006, intc_2024_1_D015) focus on Intel's x86 ecosystem strategy and foundry business model respectively. They do not provide a comparable description of a data center product portfolio specifically optimized for AI and HPC acceleration in the same context as NVIDIA's data center platform overview, which emphasizes accelerated computing vs. CPU-only approaches.

comparisons.peer_summary: CNBU data center sales were driven by server demand in cloud and enterprise markets, with growth fueled by the shift of infrastructure and workloads to the cloud and the memory-intensive nature of AI data-centric workloads.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures identify the shift of infrastructure and workloads to the cloud and the specific demands of AI workloads as primary growth drivers in the data center market. NVIDIA highlights that its Data Center platform accelerates compute-intensive workloads like AI, delivering better performance and power efficiency for these tasks. Micron similarly notes that data center sales are driven by server demand in cloud markets, where the memory-intensive nature of AI data-centric workloads requires increasing quantities of memory (DRAM/HBM) to turn data into insight. While NVIDIA focuses on the compute acceleration aspect of AI, Micron focuses on the underlying memory storage demands required to support these same AI and cloud workloads.

sentences.text: The NVIDIA Data Center platform is focused on accelerating the most compute-intensive workloads, such as AI, data analytics, graphics and scientific computing, delivering significantly better performance and power efficiency relative to conventional CPU-only approaches.
It is deployed in cloud, hyperscale, on-premises and edge data centers.
Data center: CNBU sales to the data center end market were driven primarily by server demand across the cloud and enterprise markets and solutions offered to the networking market.

Cloud servers supporting AI and data-centric workloads require significantly increasing quantities of DRAM, including HBM, and NAND as the task of turning data into insight becomes increasingly memory-centric.

peer_results.rationale: The provided candidates (qcom_2024_1_D024, qcom_2024_1_D051) focus on Industrial IoT applications and acquisitions/investments in mobile/automotive chipsets. These topics are unrelated to the data center AI and HPC compute acceleration platform described in NVIDIA's Item 1.
